task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: How does nuclear fusion work, and why has it taken so long to generate useful power from it? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of November 19, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Nuclear fusion is the process by which two light atomic nuclei merge to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy; it is the reaction that powers the sun.
The most studied fusion reaction for energy purposes combines deuterium and tritium, both isotopes of hydrogen; this reaction releases a helium nucleus and a high-energy neutron.

To fuse, nuclei must be brought close enough for the strong nuclear force to overcome their natural electrostatic repulsion; this requires temperatures above 100 million degrees Celsius, hotter than the sun's core.
At those temperatures, matter exists as a plasma — a diffuse gas of charged particles; confining plasma without any physical wall touching it is one of the central engineering challenges.
The tokamak design confines plasma in a doughnut-shaped magnetic field; the word is a Russian acronym for 'toroidal chamber with magnetic coils.'
Fusion produces no carbon dioxide and generates no long-lived radioactive waste; the primary radioactive byproduct, tritium, has a half-life of 12.3 years.
Deuterium is abundant in seawater at approximately one part in 6,400; tritium must be bred in the reactor from lithium using the neutrons produced by fusion reactions.
The key performance benchmark is called Q: the ratio of energy out to energy in; a Q above 1 means the reaction produces more energy than it consumes.
The U.S. National Ignition Facility reported a Q greater than 1 for a brief laser-driven implosion in December 2022; that experiment used an inertial confinement method, not a tokamak.
Sustained Q greater than 1 in a tokamak, for a duration useful to a power plant, has not yet been achieved by any facility.

Physicist Dr. Rena Whitfield of Lakeshore University said: "The joke used to be that commercial fusion is 30 years away and always will be. The honest answer is we're closer than ever, but closer doesn't yet mean soon."
ITER, an international experimental tokamak under construction in France since 2013, is designed to reach Q of 10 — ten times more energy out than in — but is not designed to generate electricity.
ITER is scheduled for first plasma in 2025 and full-power deuterium-tritium experiments by the mid-2030s; the project has experienced cost overruns and schedule delays.
More than 30 private companies are pursuing commercial fusion timelines; most project operational plants between 2035 and 2050.

Alternative confinement approaches include stellarators, which use complex twisted coils instead of plasma current to confine the plasma; they are less prone to instability but more difficult to engineer.

The biggest unsolved engineering problems include: maintaining plasma for hours or days rather than seconds; breeding enough tritium inside the reactor to sustain itself; and harvesting heat from high-energy neutrons without degrading structural materials.
Fusion's energy advantage over fission is that fuel is abundant and waste is manageable; the disadvantage is that it is far harder to sustain the reaction.
Dr. Whitfield said the most optimistic credible commercial timeline requires solving tritium breeding and plasma stability simultaneously, which no facility has yet done at scale.

High-temperature superconducting magnets, now commercially available, allow tokamaks to be built smaller while generating the field strength previously requiring much larger machines — a development private companies cite as genuinely new.
Fusion energy would not require the continuous fuel chain of fossil power plants; a pellet of deuterium-tritium fuel the size of a marble contains the energy equivalent of roughly 45 tons of coal.

forbidden_additions: a claim that commercial fusion power already exists
a Q value different from those in the notes
a description of ITER as generating electricity
